### zBuild — Vision

> The North Star for zBuild — it steers how zBuild is built. The README distills it; the wiki references it; every pipeline run is steered by it.

#### Intent
zBuild turns a delivery process into data — templates and plugins — so software is built the same disciplined way every time. We build zBuild the way zBuild builds: a minimal core, with all behavior plugin-delivered and template-composed. A good change is small, aligned to the spec, proven by a test, and wired into the live path — never scaffolding that looks finished but does nothing.

#### Principles
- **Target-agnostic by contract** — zBuild builds *any* repository, not itself; the engine and plugins never assume the target's language, layout, or that zBuild is the target. Target knowledge lives in data — templates, config, per-repo overrides — never in code.
- **Spec wins over drift** — KEEPERS, ARCHITECTURE, and the ADRs are the source of truth; when code disagrees, the code changes, not the spec.
- **Small engine, behavior at the edges** — keep the core tiny; add capability as plugins composed in templates, never by growing the engine.
- **Safety is structural** — all model-bound text passes one redaction chokepoint; state is atomic and resumable; scope is governed at every boundary.
- **Models are data, not code** — selection flows through the router and config tiers; never hardcode a model name.
- **Prove behavior, then wire it** — every change ships a test that fails without it and connects to the live path; green-but-inert is a defect.
- **Fail closed, never silent** — gates block on real problems and say why; bounded cycles and recovery drive work to done.
- **Dogfood every change** — build zBuild with zBuild; if the pipeline can't ship it, fix the pipeline.

### Rules
These are this repository's rules (.zbuild/prompts/rules.md). Work that
breaks one is wrong, whoever wrote it.

- Bash only, and match the file you are in: 4-space indent, LF line endings, a final newline, no trailing whitespace (.editorconfig). Everything must pass `shellcheck` with the repo's .shellcheckrc.
- Never pipe anything into `grep -q`, and never pipe into a bare `head`, in any `.sh` file, test files included. The reader exits early, the writer takes SIGPIPE, and under `set -o pipefail` the line fails for a reason nothing logs. Use a here-string instead: `grep -q PATTERN <<< "$var"`, or run grep on the file directly: `grep -q PATTERN "$file"`. `tests/unit/sigpipe-antipattern-guard-test.sh` fails the suite on any violation; a genuinely safe pipe is annotated `# sigpipe-ok: <reason>`.
- Never name a model (haiku, sonnet, opus, …) in code; model selection goes through core/router and config/models.json.
- A test must be able to fail: assert what is required, never what the code happens to do.
- Never edit anything under `legacy-DoNotUse/`.

#### Facts about this repo
- `ZBUILD_*` environment variables are set by the engine at dispatch (the artifact dir, the stage's input index `ZBUILD_STAGE_INPUTS`, the issue, the run). They are trusted engine inputs, not user or attacker input.
- A stage never names another stage's output — not its output name, not its file. The engine hands every stage every earlier stage's latest output, and a stage finds what it needs by what it contains (scripts/lib/earlier-output.sh; ADR-055 §1). A plugin that names another stage's output is a defect.
- Every stage writes a v2 result (`result_contract`, `verdict`, `disposition`, `reason`, detail under `data`) on every exit path, and exits 0 or 1 (ADR-054).
- `[SPEC-n]` / `[#<issue>/SPEC-n]` tags in a test tie an assertion to one issue's acceptance contract. A tag that belongs to another issue must never be changed or removed.

This repository's guidance for this stage (.zbuild/prompts/design-overrides.md).
It adds to your job; it cannot take any part of it away.

### zBuild design-stage scope overrides

Per-repo overlay to the generic design charter's "enumerated set / absence-by-
omission" principle (ADR-032/033). The shipped engine states the principle; this
file states this repo's genuine domain-specific enumerations that break by
OMISSION. Consult this when a change grows, shrinks, or renames a closed set in
this repository.

> **ADR-047 tombstone (EPIC #1277 / #1282).** zBuild's pipeline stage set is NO
> LONGER a closed, engine-owned vocabulary. `_ZBUILD_CANONICAL_STAGES` was
> demoted (ADR-047 §5): stage membership is now a manifest-derived, fail-closed
> resolvability preflight and stage ordering a data-dependency DAG — both keyed
> on declared data, not a hardcoded roster. The former Rules ABS-1/ABS-2/ABS-3
> here enumerated that now-open roster and are retired. What remains below is the
> **generic** principle only (it names no stage), plus this repo's real closed
> sets. A change that adds/removes/renames a pipeline stage is now a template +
> plugin change; it no longer breaks an engine-owned roster enumeration.

#### Rule ABS — generic enumerated-set / absence-by-omission wisdom

Some closed sets in this repo break by OMISSION rather than by a stale token you
can grep: the breakage is a MISSING (or orphaned) line, not a changed one. When a
change grows, shrinks, or renames such a set, every enumeration of that set is
wrong by omission — yet there is nothing to grep for, because the defect is the
absent entry.

When a change touches a genuinely-closed, exhaustively-enumerated set in this
repo, design MUST include in scope every test or config that enumerates or COUNTS
that set. Because the breakage is an absence, do not trust a hardcoded list of
sites to stay complete — rediscover the sites each time (see "How to find them").

This principle is target-agnostic: it applies to any closed set, and it does not
presume the pipeline stage set is closed (per the ADR-047 tombstone above, it is
not). Use it for sets that are genuinely closed in this repo, declared here per
ADR-032 as this repo's domain-specific enumerations.

#### How to find them

Enumeration/count sites are most often mock-plugin roster blocks (one call per
member) or literal counts of the set. Rediscover them with:

```
grep -rln '_make_plugin\|_make_role_plugin\|_make_verdict_plugin\|mock_plugin_factory' tests/
grep -rln 'stage\.complete\|plugin\.run\.start\|started .*UTC\|finished .*UTC' tests/
```

Every match that enumerates or counts a closed set you are changing belongs in
the design scope block. Re-run the greps each time — new enumeration sites arrive
with new tests, and the defect (a missing line) leaves no token to search for.

#### Rule ABS-W — new plugin directory requires a wiki page

Any change that creates `plugins/<kind>/<id>/manifest.yaml` MUST include
`docs/wiki/plugins/<id>.md` in scope. The `lint-doc-freshness` gate
(`scripts/lib/lint-doc-freshness.sh`) enforces this at test time against the
real repo tree — it fails if the wiki page is absent or lacks a prose opening
paragraph. This is an absence-by-omission gap: there is no old value to grep
for, because the defect is the missing new file.

**Exception — `kind: persona` plugins:** `kind: persona` manifests are
data-only (no `plugin.sh`, no hooks) and share a single index page at
`docs/wiki/plugins/personas.md`. Adding a new persona requires editing
`docs/wiki/plugins/personas.md` to list the new id (one known, stable file)
rather than creating a per-id page. The `lint-doc-freshness` gate enforces
that `personas.md` exists and that every persona id appears as a literal
string in it; per-id pages for personas are not required and will trigger
orphan failures if present.

## What you own

Your job: write the design — the change's decisions and its acceptance contract — in the working copy at the path below. When it passes design's checks it becomes design.md. Save it as you go: a design on disk when your time runs out still counts.

The working copy already holds YOUR LATEST DESIGN (below). Change only what needs to change.

Previous work may hold findings from later stages. A finding is yours only if changing the design would fix it: its acceptance contract. Answer each of those in the design. Leave the others — a bug in the code, a test that does not run, a lint failure — and do not investigate them. In a Findings section of the design, list every finding: what you changed for it, or why you left it. You do not debug code or work out why a test fails.

Write the design document to this EXACT absolute path:
  /home/runner/work/_temp/zbuild-state/artifacts/design-draft.md

The design document MUST include:
1. A brief architectural decision summary (goal, context, decision).
2. A ```steps block: the ordered work items that deliver the change, one per
   line, each with the areas of the code it is about:
```steps
- <what to do, in one sentence> | areas: path/to/file1, path/to/file2
```
   The build follows them in order.

3. A ```acceptance block listing what this change must deliver. Each line is
   one requirement: an id, a status, and ONE behaviour someone could observe and test.
   The id describes the SPEC: DS, then 3 or 4 capital letters or digits,
   starting with a letter, that say what it is about, a dash, and a number —
   DSLOOP-1 for a SPEC about loop state. The id is also the tag its test
   carries, [DSLOOP-1], so it must be new to the repository:
   - A new SPEC's number is one more than the highest number already used
     with the same letters in any test file in the repository. If tests
     already hold DSLOOP-1 and DSLOOP-3, the new one is DSLOOP-4, and the
     next is DSLOOP-5.
   - A SPEC you keep keeps its id.
   - A SPEC you drop gets a line `REMOVED: <id> — <why>`, kept in every later
     design, so its id is never used again.
   - Never use one of the issue's requirement ids as a SPEC id.
   A design written with old ids (SPEC-1, or ids not starting with DS) gives
   each SPEC a new id once; the old ids need no REMOVED line.
   A requirement that asks for several things gets one SPEC per thing, each
   naming the same requirement id in covers: — never one SPEC that joins them with "and" or ";".
   Each SPEC is checked against one assertion, so a SPEC that promises two
   things is never fully met by it.

   Under its line, each [code] and [done] SPEC says its behaviour in parts, one
   per line, indented ([no-code] may too):
   - `Given:` the setup the behaviour starts from. Optional; any number.
   - `When:` the one action — exactly one When per SPEC: a second action is a second SPEC.
   - `Then:` something a test can observe after the When — an output, a
     result, a file the code writes, an event. One or more. Never what a file
     or a test contains.
   - `And:` adds another line to the Given, Then or Cleanup above it.
   - `Cleanup:` what must be true again after the test, for anything the
     Given sets up or a Then says happens that outlives the test — an exported
     variable, a file outside the test's own folder, global config or git state.
     Leave it out when nothing outlives the test: the test harness cleans up
     after every test.

   The status says what work the requirement needs. Look at the code before you choose:
   - `DSLOOP-1[code]:` — it needs code. Its test must fail on the code as it is before your change, and pass after it.
     If the code already does it, it is not [code]: its test would already pass, and the build stalls on it.
     Every requirement except a [doc] one describes what someone could see happen, not what a file contains: not "x.sh contains foo", "file y exists" or "the test file has both cases" — no test can prove those.
   - `DSLOOP-2[no-code]:` — it needs work that changes no behaviour: a test,
     config, or a refactor. Its test must pass after the change; it need not fail before.
   - `DSDOCS-1[doc]:` — it changes a doc. It has no test and no Given/When/Then: say, on its one line, what the doc must tell a reader
     (the guide says a resume puts back what every finished stage wrote). The doc is read to check it.
   - `DSGARD-1[done]:` — the code from before your change already does it. Name the evidence at the end of the line, after ` evidence: ` —
     a file by its path from the repository root, then ` | `, then one line of it copied as it is
     (scripts/x.sh | run_guard()), or an existing test file named alone.
     The text must be in the file on the commit this branch started from: code this work added is not
     done yet, so it is [code]. A [done] SPEC still gets a test: it must pass after the change, and it
     need not fail before — it proves the finished change still does what the old code did.
   Every requirement carries one of the four. A change that edits code needs at least one [code] requirement.

   You name no files: no test file, and no list of the files the change
   touches. The tests are written after the design, in the repository's test
   folders, wherever they belong, and a requirement's test is found by its
   tag. Each [code] assertion is also run against the code from before your
   change and must fail there, so write ONE requirement per assertion — then
   each behaviour is checked on its own.

The ```acceptance block format:
```acceptance
DSLOOP-1[code]: <one new behaviour this change introduces>
  Given: <the setup it starts from>
  When: <the one action>
  Then: <what a test can observe after it>
  And: <another thing a test can observe>
  Cleanup: <what must be true again after, when the setup or a Then outlives the test>
DSLOOP-2[no-code]: <a test, config or a refactor that changes no behaviour>
DSDOCS-1[doc]: <what a doc must tell a reader>
DSGARD-1[done]: <something the code already does> evidence: scripts/x.sh | run_guard()
  When: <the action>
  Then: <what the code from before this change already does>
REMOVED: DSLOOP-3 — <why this SPEC was dropped>
WIRING: <the existing file that calls the new code>
```

WIRING: Which existing file calls the new code?
- Name the existing file whose code calls (or loads) the new behaviour:
  the place a running program reaches it from. It is not the file that
  implements the behaviour, and it is not a test. If that file were put back
  to how it is today, at least one test of this change would fail.
- A list, schema or config entry is never this file: adding a name to an event
  list, a schema or a config list changes no behaviour on its own.
- One path per line; several lines are allowed:
    WIRING:
    plugins/agent/build/plugin.sh
    core/pipeline/runner.sh
- If nothing calls the new code yet (a helper used later), write
  `WIRING: none`.
- After the build, the file you name is put back to its old version (everything
  else kept), and at least one test must then fail. That is how the pipeline
  checks you named the right file.

Existing checks this change makes wrong: when the change alters a
behaviour an EXISTING assertion pins (one that is not a SPEC of this contract),
list it in a ```supersedes block — one line per check, the testfile path,
the assertion's tag, and why it is now wrong:
```supersedes
tests/unit/foo-test.sh [SPEC-3]: `verdict` is now the v2 result's status key, not a merge decision
```
Updating those checks to the new behaviour is part of writing the tests. Omit
the block when no existing check changes meaning.

A requirement you do not understand — the issue could mean either of two
things — is not guessed in silence. Write one line for it in the design,
outside the fenced blocks:
UNCLEAR: <id> | <the question> | <what you assumed>
where <id> is the requirement's id. Then carry on with that assumption: design
the change as if it were the answer. The question and your assumption are
shown to the people who can answer it.

Keep the prose focused and under 200 lines (the acceptance block may be as
long as completeness requires).

The issue may describe a solution as well as the
problem. A section that records a decision (for example "Decision:") is binding: follow it.
Anything else it proposes — an approach, a file list, a claim that

### The code from before this change
The commit this branch started from is a copy at /home/runner/work/_temp/zbuild-state/base-code. A [done] SPEC is checked
there: to see whether the code from before your change already does something,
open the file there, not in the working copy — the working copy holds every

### Requirements from the issue (each with its id)
- RQRESU-1: A resume trusts every stage that already ran.
- RQRESU-2: Each stage the interrupted run completed counts as done, and its outputs are put back (rehydrated) exactly as they were when the run stopped.
- RQRESU-3: The run picks up at the stage that was interrupted, which runs again from its start.
- RQFROM-1: `--from-stage <s>` works the same way: every stage before `<s>` is trusted and rehydrated, and the run starts at `<s>`.
- RQADR-1: Amend ADR-006 (resume contract) with the decision above, with the amendment naming its enforcing tests inline.
- RQADR-2: Amend ADR-050 §6 to draw the line explicitly, stating that the rule "never skip a stage on the basis of prior output" governs a **new** run reusing an **earlier run's** work and stays, while resume continues **the same run** and is governed by ADR-006, with a test pinning each side.
- RQHYDR-1: Rehydration follows the same path the hydrate stage already uses (ADR-050, `plugins/tool/hydrate`), so "exactly as before" means the same files at the same paths.
- RQLOOP-1: Inside a loop (e.g. build → test), a run interrupted mid-round resumes at the interrupted stage of that round. The loop's iteration count and state are restored, not reset.
- RQFROM-2: `--from-stage <s>` dispatches `<s>` first, with every earlier stage's outputs rehydrated. It never emits `pipeline.skip_to_stage` and then runs an earlier stage.
- RQFROM-3: `--from-stage <s>` naming a stage with no prior output to rehydrate refuses with a reason, and does not start.
- RQFROM-4: `--from-stage <s>` works only when `--resume` is given. Without `--resume` the run refuses with a reason ("only valid with --resume") and does not start, even when the run would otherwise resume by itself.
- RQPATH-1: Every way to resume (`--resume`, auto-resume on restart, and `zbuild pipeline resume --run-id`) finds the interrupted run's state in `runs/<run_id>/` and behaves as RQRESU-4. Each has its own test.
- RQGUAR-1: A run with no prior state behaves exactly as today. This is a guard.
- RQGUAR-2: A **new** run of the same issue still never skips a stage because of an earlier run's output (ADR-050 §6). This is a guard.

Every requirement above must be covered by at least one SPEC. End each SPEC line with ` covers: ` and the ids of the requirements it covers, before any ` evidence: ` — for example `DSLOOP-1[code]: <behaviour> covers: <requirement ids>`. A requirement the code already meets is covered by a [done] SPEC with evidence.

### YOUR LATEST DESIGN (refine it; Previous work says what moved since you wrote it)
Every claim it makes about the repository — an ADR it relies on, a file it lists, a hook, field or convention it declares — is re-checked against the tree as it is NOW, and every SPEC it keeps against the issue's requirements as they are NOW, not only the new ones: anything that no longer holds is dropped or re-derived — a SPEC a requirement now contradicts is rewritten or removed — and the design says what changed and why. Keep what still holds; do not start over.

# Design: #1805 — resume and --from-stage trust-and-rehydrate

## Architectural decision

**Goal:** When a run is resumed (via `--resume`, auto-resume on restart, or `zbuild pipeline resume --run-id`), every stage already marked `complete` in the persisted state must have its artifacts restored from the git state branch into `ZBUILD_ARTIFACT_DIR` before the dispatch loop runs, using the same extraction path the hydrate plugin uses. After that restoration, a `complete` stage whose primary artifact is still absent must exit 1 (fail closed). For `--from-stage <s>`, the same rehydration runs for every stage before `<s>`; if any pre-target stage has no restorable artifact, the runner refuses before dispatching anything. Inside a loop, the cycle orchestrator must restore `cycle_iterations[X].current_iter` from persisted state and begin the iteration loop from that value, not from 1, but ONLY when a resume is active — fresh runs must always start from iter=1. Additionally, within the first resumed iteration, `_cycle_dispatch` must skip cycle member stages already marked complete in persisted state and explicitly emit stage.start for the interrupted (non-complete) member, so the first dispatched cycle member is the one that was actually interrupted.

**Context / gaps (verified against current tree):**
- Gap 1 — runner.sh resume entry: disarms sentinel, emits `pipeline.resume`, NO artifact restoration. **Fixed** — `_runner_resume_rehydrate` (new function in runner.sh), called from `main()` in runner.sh at the resume entry point.
- Gap 2 — runner.sh stale-artifact branch warned+continued; after rehydration the right behaviour is exit 1. **Fixed** — exit 1 path in the dispatch-unit `stage:*` arm inside `main()` in runner.sh (comment: "ADR-006 §3.6 (#1805): fail closed").
- Gap 3 — runner.sh from-stage path: no artifact check or rehydration. **Fixed** — `_runner_from_stage_preflight` (new function in runner.sh).
- Gap 4 — `_cycle_orchestrator_run_body` reads `current_iter` unconditionally, breaking nested loops. **Fixed** — `_cycle_orchestrator_run_body()` in cycle-orchestrator.sh wraps the `_persisted_iter` read with `if [[ ${_ZBUILD_RESUME_ACTIVE:-false} == true ]]; then`; flag is consumed immediately after reading (`_ZBUILD_RESUME_ACTIVE=false`, comment: "Consume the flag: nested cycles and subsequent re-entries start at 1"); fresh/nested-loop re-entries take the else branch setting `_start_iter=1`.
- Gap 5 — dispatch-unit loop (cycle:* arm, stage:* arm) lacked skip-on-complete guard for resume mode; only the legacy linear loop had one. **Fixed** — guards in `main()` in runner.sh: dispatch-unit `cycle:*` arm and dispatch-unit `stage:*` arm, both conditioned on `$resume_mode`; added by this branch.
- Gap 6 — ADR-006 and ADR-050 not amended. **Fixed in implementation.**
- Gap 7 — An unconditional `_cd_iter > 0` guard was added inside `_cycle_dispatch()` in runner.sh to emit `stage.start` for all cycle member dispatches. This is WRONG: `_cd_iter` starts at 1 and only increases, so the guard fires on every dispatch in every run (fresh and resume). Issue-acceptance finding 2 confirms this changes fresh-run event sequences and breaks `tests/golden/full-pipeline/event-sequence.golden` and `tests/golden/parity/event-sequence.golden`, violating RQGUAR-1. Stage.start for the interrupted cycle member during resume does NOT require an unconditional guard — it must be emitted by the DSCMBR-1 `resume_first_iter=true` path: when `resume_first_iter=true` and the cycle member is not marked complete (the interrupted member), `_cycle_dispatch` explicitly emits `stage.start` for that member before dispatching. For fresh runs and later resumed iterations (`resume_first_iter=false` or not set), `_cycle_dispatch` preserves pre-branch behavior: no stage.start emission for cycle members through this code path. If the branch added the `_cd_iter > 0` guard, it must be removed.
- Gap 8 — The auto-resume elif branch inside `main()` in runner.sh tests `[[ -f "$state_file" ]]` where `state_file = $state_dir/pipeline-state.json` (the flat default root path). But the per-run layout (ADR-059 §1) stores state at `runs/<run_id>/pipeline-state.json`, not at the root. The `latest` symlink at `$(zbuild_layout_state_root)/latest` points to the most-recent per-run dir and is already used by `_find_state_file` in `scripts/zbuild`, but runner.sh's auto-resume check never consults it. Result: without ZBUILD_STATE_FILE set, auto-resume never fires for any per-run default layout. All existing auto-resume tests mask this gap by setting ZBUILD_STATE_FILE explicitly. **NOT YET FIXED** — extend the auto-resume elif to check `$state_dir/latest/pipeline-state.json` when the flat path does not exist, and update state_dir/state_file to the resolved per-run path when `auto_resume` fires (step 7b).
- Gap 9 — Within the first resumed iteration (iter k), member stages already marked complete must be skipped so the first dispatched member is the interrupted stage. DSSKIP-1's dispatch-unit skip guard applies to top-level `_TPL_DISPATCH_UNITS` entries only; `_cycle_dispatch` is called from inside the cycle orchestrator and has no equivalent guard. **NOT YET FIXED** — the cycle orchestrator must signal to `_cycle_dispatch` whether it is dispatching the first resumed iteration, and `_cycle_dispatch` must skip members already marked complete and explicitly emit stage.start for the non-complete (interrupted) member (step for DSCMBR-1).
- Gap 10 — `pipeline.skip_to_stage` emission in combined resume+from-stage mode. The `pipeline.skip_to_stage` emission inside `main()` in runner.sh fires whenever `--from-stage` is active, including when `--resume` is also active. RQFROM-2 says the event must not be FOLLOWED BY running an earlier stage — that constraint is met because the rehydration path and dispatch-loop skip guards prevent earlier-stage dispatch in both pure from-stage and resume+from-stage modes. The event's emission in combined mode is therefore RQFROM-2-compliant; DSFSTG-1 makes this explicit via a Then clause. No code change is required for this gap — the existing behavior satisfies RQFROM-2.
- Gap 11 — In combined `--resume --from-stage <s>` mode, once the target unit is found and `skip_until_stage` is cleared, `resume_mode` remains `true`. Every subsequent dispatch-unit loop iteration then has `resume_mode=true && skip_until_stage=""`, which triggers the resume skip guard for all units after `<s>`. Any unit after `<s>` that is marked complete in the interrupted run's state will therefore be skipped — but RQFROM-1 says "the run starts at `<s>`", which requires all stages from `<s>` onward to be dispatched. **NOT YET FIXED** — in both arms, immediately after clearing `skip_until_stage`, also set `resume_mode=false` immediately: `[[ -n "$skip_until_stage" ]] && { skip_until_stage=""; resume_mode=false; }` — this prevents the resume skip guard from activating for stages after `<s>` in combined `--resume --from-stage <s>` mode; pure resume runs (no from-stage) never set `skip_until_stage`, so this line is never reached and `resume_mode` is unaffected.
- Gap 12 — The `--from-stage` validation guard was moved by this branch to run AFTER the auto-resume check. This violates RQFROM-4. In the base code the guard ran before auto-resume; the branch moved it after, allowing auto-resume + --from-stage without explicit --resume. Additionally, the branch introduced a "narrowed" pre-auto-resume guard (interrupted-status only) and a `skip_restore=false` path in `_runner_from_stage_preflight` to allow `--from-stage` without `--resume` for `in_progress` states — this is also a RQFROM-4 violation. **NOT YET FIXED** — (a) move the guard back to execute immediately after argument parsing and before the auto-resume elif check (restoring base-code behavior), without any status narrowing: `if [[ -n "$from_stage" ]] && ! $resume_mode; then error "--from-stage is only valid with --resume"; fi` — this guard fires for ALL states, regardless of status=interrupted or status=in_progress; (b) remove the `skip_restore=false` path of `_runner_from_stage_preflight` — it is dead code per RQFROM-4: `_runner_from_stage_preflight` is only ever called after the guard has confirmed `resume_mode=true`, so `skip_restore=false` is unreachable; (c) update S5 in from-stage-rehydrate-test.sh (the sub-case currently using `--from-stage cyc` without `--resume` with `in_progress` state) to use `--resume --from-stage cyc` instead — it tests the same rehydration behavior (DSFSTG-1) and its assertions about artifact restoration remain valid when invoked with explicit `--resume`.

**Decision:**
Extract the copy logic from `_hydrate_put_back` (plugins/tool/hydrate/plugin.sh) into `_artifact_persist_put_back <from> <to>` in `core/state/artifact-persist.sh`. Redirect hydrate's `hydrate_run` call site to the new function. At the resume entry point in runner.sh, export `_ZBUILD_RESUME_ACTIVE=true` (already set inside `main()`, immediately after the `_runner_resume_rehydrate` call).
